471.quote_or_event: “No power to speak, no power to keep silent. … He alone has the Power in His Hands. He watches over all.”
471.explanation: In the thirty-third pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak denies that any human has power of their own, even to speak or keep silent; all power is in God's hand.
471.tie_back: The Kural tells the actor to weigh the strengths of task, self, enemy and allies; Guru Nanak teaches that every such strength finally rests with God.
471.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (pauri 33), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
471._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both concern the measure of power, but Japji relativizes all human strength to God rather than advising how to compare strengths.

472.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
472.explanation: In Gujri Ki Vaar Guru Arjan praises udam, steady effort, and practice kept up over time as the way to life and peace.
472.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is out of reach for those who know what they can do and keep steadily at it; Guru Arjan likewise promises the fruit of sustained effort.
472.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
472._accuracy_note: Good on persistent effort; the effort meant is remembrance of God, and the Kural's first step, knowing one's own capacity, is absent.

473.quote_or_event: “My strength is exhausted, and I am in bondage; I cannot do anything at all.”
473.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur gives voice to someone whose strength has run out and who is left helpless and bound.
473.tie_back: The Kural speaks of those who misjudged their strength and broke down midway; Guru Tegh Bahadur describes that state of spent strength and helplessness.
473.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 53), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
473._accuracy_note: Partial: it describes exhausted strength, not misjudged strength, and the salok's remedy is reliance on God rather than measuring oneself beforehand.

474.quote_or_event: “The humble beings abide in peace; subduing egotism, they are meek. The very proud and arrogant persons, O Nanak, are consumed by their own pride.”
474.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan contrasts the humble, who live in peace, with the proud, who are destroyed by their own pride (haumai).
474.tie_back: The Kural says the self-admiring man who ignores his own measure soon comes to ruin; Guru Arjan says the arrogant are consumed by their pride.
474.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (ashtapadi 12, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
474._accuracy_note: A strong fit on self-admiration leading to ruin; the Kural also faults failing to accommodate others and not knowing one's strength, which this verse does not address.

475.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books. … O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
475.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak imagines learning piled up by the cartload (gadee) and says that without the one thing, the Name, it all counts for nothing.
475.tie_back: The Kural pictures a cart overloaded even with feathers; Guru Nanak also pictures a cart piled with light things, though his point is their worthlessness, not the breaking axle.
475.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
475._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the cartload image is shared, but Guru Nanak's lesson (piled learning is empty without the Name) differs from the Kural's (small things in excess break the strongest).

476.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, do not be so proud of your tall mansions. Today or tomorrow, you shall lie beneath the ground, and the grass shall grow above you.”
476.explanation: In a salok in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir warns that whatever height one reaches is temporary and the fall to the ground is sure.
476.tie_back: The Kural warns that climbing beyond the branch tip is fatal; Kabir warns that those proud of their height will soon lie low.
476.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1366, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 38) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
476._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both warn about overreaching height, but Kabir speaks of death's leveling of all pride, not of pushing past the limit of one's strength.

477.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
477.explanation: Guru Nanak joins honest earning (kirat karni) with sharing (vand chhakna): one gives some of what one has earned, not all of it.
477.tie_back: The Kural says to give in the right way, knowing the measure of one's means, so that wealth is preserved while given; Guru Nanak commends giving a part of honest earnings.
477.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
477._accuracy_note: A strong fit: giving a portion of honest earnings balances charity and livelihood; the Kural's explicit stress on measuring one's means is only implied.

478.quote_or_event: “I ask for two kilos of flour, and half a pound of ghee, and salt.”
478.explanation: In Raag Sorath Bhagat Kabir lists the plain needs he asks of God: a little flour, a little ghee and salt, nothing beyond.
478.tie_back: The Kural says a small income does no harm if spending stays within it; Kabir's modest list shows needs kept small.
478.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
478._accuracy_note: Partial: it models modest consumption, but it is a devotee's prayer for sustenance, not a teaching on matching outflow to income.

479.quote_or_event: “As the bubbles in the water well up and disappear again, so is the universe created; says Nanak, listen, O my friend!”
479.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur compares worldly existence to a bubble that rises and vanishes on the water.
479.tie_back: The Kural says the life of one who lives beyond his means seems to prosper, then vanishes without a trace; Guru Tegh Bahadur's bubble has the same brief show and quick end.
479.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 25), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
479._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the image of seeming then vanishing fits, but the salok is about the transience of the whole world, not the spendthrift's ruin.

480.quote_or_event: Sikhs practice dasvandh, setting aside a tenth of their earnings in the Guru's name for the community's common resources. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism traces the idea to Guru Nanak's line on earning and sharing (Ang 1245) and records that under Guru Ram Das Sikhs were asked to set apart at least ten per cent of their income for the common pool.
480.explanation: Dasvandh gives Sikh generosity a set proportion, so that giving is regular and tied to what one actually earns.
480.tie_back: The Kural warns that generosity that does not weigh one's resources soon exhausts wealth; dasvandh ties giving to a fixed share of income.
480.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala), "Dasvandh" by Wazir Singh (paraphrase)
480._accuracy_note: Reasonable: dasvandh measures giving by income, but it is a minimum obligation rather than a cap, and Gurbani itself never warns against giving too much.
